COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Blair Wilson, the plaintiff by counterclaim in
this defamation action, applies to strike significant portions of the
defendants’ Statements of Defence under R. 9‑5(1) of the
Supreme Court
Civil Rules
. He argues that the defences of justification, fair comment,
and fair reporting should be struck based on the application of the doctrines
of either
res judicata
or abuse of process.

[
2
]

In a prior proceeding, Mr. Wilson’s wife, Kelly
Wilson sought a variation of her late mother’s will in her favour pursuant to
the
Wills Variation Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 490 (the “
WVA
Action”).
Ms. Wilson’s mother, the late Norma Lougheed, died on May 24, 2007. Ms. Wilson,
who was Mrs. Lougheed’s only child, brought the
WVA
Action against her father,
William Lougheed, both in his personal capacity and as the executor of Mrs.
Lougheed’s estate (the “Estate”). The reasons for judgment of Ballance J. in
those proceedings are indexed at
2010 BCSC 1868
(the “Reasons”).

[
3
]

In a counterclaim to the
WVA
Action, as
well as in a separate debt action (the “Debt Action”), Mr. Lougheed in his
personal and representative capacities and as the directing mind of the
Lougheeds’ private company, Norbill Investments Ltd. (Norbill Investments),
sought to recover monies allegedly loaned to Ms. and Mr. Wilson primarily to
facilitate the acquisition of six parcels of real property in British Columbia.
In the Reasons Ballance J. referred to the six properties by their respective
locations: the Jefferson Avenue property, the Gordon Avenue property, the
Lawson Avenue property, the Pemberton Valley property, the Whistler property,
and the Roberts Creek property. For convenience in these reasons I will
reference to the six properties in the same manner. Ms. and Mr. Wilson were
both named as defendants in the Debt Action.

[
4
]

Shortly after the
WVA
Action was
commenced, Mr. Lougheed was widely quoted on the subject of the debt
allegations and other matters in an October 28, 2007 article about Mr. Wilson
in
The Province
(the “Article”), entitled “Family exposes MP’s trail of
debt”. The Article gave rise to the present action in defamation (the “Defamation
Action”). The claim was initiated as a counterclaim by Mr. Wilson to the Debt
Action. The terms of a
consent order dated November 4,
2009, provided that the
WVA
Action and the claims in the Debt Action
against Ms. Wilson be tried at the same time. Pursuant to a subsequent consent
order dated November 12, 2009, (the “Consent Order”) the Defamation Action,
along with Mr. Lougheed’s claims against Mr. Wilson in the Debt Action, was
severed from that proceeding.

[
5
]

The claims in the Debt Action against Ms. Wilson
and the Counterclaim in the
WVA
Action were overlapping. Prior to the
trial in the
WVA
Action, Mr. Lougheed discontinued his claim in the Debt
Action for repayment of the alleged loans in respect of the Jefferson Avenue,
Gordon Avenue, and Lawson Avenue properties. However, at trial Mr. Lougheed
pursued the debt allegations against Ms. Wilson in relation to the Gordon Avenue
and Lawson Avenue properties by way of his counterclaim in the
WVA
Action.
He discontinued those claims when Ms. Wilson closed her case at trial. Madam
Justice Ballance adjudicated upon the claims in the Debt Action regarding Ms.
Wilson’s indebtedness with respect to the Whistler and Roberts Creek properties.
For the sake of convenience, the debt claim against Ms. Wilson heard by
Ballance J.

and Ms. Wilson’s claim under the
WVA
Action will be
referred to collectively in these reasons as the “
WVA
Action”. The
matter proceeded to a 16-day trial.

[
6
]

The record shows that in the Debt Action against
Mr. Wilson, the only extant claims relate to a $22,480.82 “loan” from Mrs.
Lougheed to Mr. Wilson, which the Article alleged Mr. Wilson requested while
Mrs. Lougheed was on her deathbed (the “Deathbed Loan”), and an alleged loan
from Mr. Lougheed to Mr. Wilson in the amount of $5,000.00.

[
7
]

In addition to Mr. Lougheed, the Defamation
Action is brought against Elaine O’Connor, the author of the Article, and
Canwest Publishing Inc. Publications Canwest Inc. the publisher of
The
Province
(collectively, the “Canwest Defendants”). The other defendants by
counterclaim are Judeline Tyabji Wilson, Tugboat Enterprises Ltd., Mark Allan
Marissen, and Steve Janke.

[
8
]

The Canwest Defendants and Mr. Lougheed opposed
this application. The other defendants by counterclaim (Judeline Tyabji Wilson,
Tugboat Enterprises Ltd., Mark Allan Marissen, and Steve Janke) did not appear or
participate in any way on this application.

POSITION OF THE PARTIES

Mr. Wilson’s Position

[
9
]

In essence on this pre-trial motion, the
applicant seeks an order that the respondents, the Canwest Defendants and Mr.
Lougheed, are precluded from relying on certain defences in the Defamation
Action because as a matter of law and/or fairness the parties are bound by the
findings of the Court in the
WVA
Action.

[
10
]

More particularly, the applicant argues that it
is plain and obvious that the doctrines of
res judicata
and abuse of
process apply to preclude the respondents from relying on the defences of
justification, fair comment, and fair reporting in the Defamation Action. To
the extent that any of these defences requires the respondents to prove the truth
of the alleged defamatory statements, the applicant submits that permitting the
respondents to call evidence regarding the debts allegedly owed by the Wilsons
to either Mr. Lougheed, the Estate or Norbill Investments in relation to the
six properties would amount to a relitigation of matters that were finally
determined in the
WVA
Action. For convenience I will refer to these
matters collectively in these reasons as the “Property Advances”.

[
11
]

The applicant’s primary contention is that the
“truth-based” defences are plainly unsustainable and should therefore be
struck. In the alternative, he seeks an order that the parties are bound by
Ballance J.’s findings in the
WVA
Action regarding the Property
Advances.

[
12
]

In the further alternative, he asks for such
orders with respect to the defences of fair comment, justification and fair
reporting as the Court considers will further the object of the
Rules

for the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of the action on its merits.

[
13
]

At the hearing of the application, Mr. Wilson’s
counsel took the alternative position that allowing the respondents to adduce
evidence which contradicts the findings in the
WVA
Action would
prejudice, embarrass, or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding and
therefore the defences ought to be struck or amended pursuant to R.
9
-
5(1)
(c). Counsel
for the respondents objected to this line of argument because R. 9-5(1)(c) was
not referenced in the Notice of Application.

[
14
]

Upon reflection I determined that in all the
circumstances it would be just and convenient to allow an amendment to the
Notice of Application to include a reference to R. 9-5(1)(c) and invited the
respondents to file written submissions on the matter.

[
15
]

At this juncture, I also note that at the
conclusion of the hearing the Court also invited supplemental written
submissions on specific questions. Those submissions were provided in
accordance with the schedule the Court directed.

[
16
]

The respondents object to the applicant’s
supplemental submissions because they assert that with the exception of seven
paragraphs, the submissions, which are 17 pages in length, are not responsive
to the questions raised by the Court. I agree.

[
17
]

With the exception of the seven paragraphs
identified by the respondents, the applicant’s supplemental submissions seek to
repeat, amplify and modify his submissions at the hearing. This is not one of
those exceptional circumstances in which the applicant should be permitted to
make further argument after the completion of oral submissions.

[
18
]

In the end, I have disregarded those portions of
the applicant’s supplemental submissions which are not responsive to the
questions posed by the Court and which do not pertain to R. 9-5(1)(c).

Position of Mr. Lougheed and the Canwest Defendants

[
19
]

The overarching submission of Mr. Lougheed and
the Canwest Defendants is that the application should be dismissed because the
applicant has not established the requisite elements for either
res judicata

or abuse of process.

[
20
]

In broad terms, the respondents’ position can be
summarized as follows:

i.

With respect to issue estoppel, they assert that
there is no mutuality between these proceedings and the
WVA
Action
because the parties to the Defamation Action are not the same as those in the
WVA

Action. Mr. Wilson himself was not a party to the
WVA
Action and
therefore he cannot complain of being “twice vexed”. The Canwest Defendants
were not parties to the
WVA
action nor are they privies of Mr. Lougheed.

ii.

With respect to abuse of process, they argue
that the tests for establishing liability in debt are different from the tests
for making out the defences of justification, fair comment, and - as it
pertains to the Canwest Defendants - fair reporting. They maintain that the
questions before the Court in these proceedings raise issues that were not
decided in the
WVA
Action. Therefore, the adjudication of the impugned defences
does not risk inefficient use of judicial resources, undermine the finality of
proceedings, or challenge the integrity of the adjudicative function of the
courts.

[
21
]

In developing their primary contention, the
respondents forcefully assert that they are not required to make out their
defences in order to defeat the present pleadings motion; rather they need only
show that it is not plain and obvious that the impugned defences are doomed to
fail.

[
22
]

Insofar as the alternative relief sought, the
Canwest Defendants submit that neither
res judicata
nor abuse of process
is applicable and, therefore, the findings in the
WVA
Action are not
binding in the Defamation Action. However, it emerged at the hearing of the
application that the Canwest Defendants do not intend to challenge Ballance
J.’s findings in the
WVA
Action. They reiterated this position in their supplemental
written submissions.

[
23
]

At the hearing Mr. Lougheed maintained that the impugned
defences do not seek to relitigate issues that were decided in the
WVA
Action.
He argues therefore that the defences should not be struck and that the parties
should not be bound by any findings in the
WVA
Action. Notably in his
supplemental written submissions he made four narrowly prescribed admissions. I
will refer to these admissions later in these reasons.

[
24
]

At this juncture I note that Mr. Lougheed’s
principal defence is his denial of any publication of the alleged defamatory
statements. He relies on the defences of justification and fair comment in the
alternative.

FACTS

[
25
]

Before turning to the analysis it is necessary
to summarize the pertinent background facts. More particularly, this
application must be considered in the context of the allegations in the
Article, the findings of the Court in the
WVA
Action, and the correction
to the Article which was published on January 23, 2011 in
The Province

(the “Correction”).

The Debt Allegations in the Article

[
26
]

The Article quotes Mr. Lougheed as alleging,
among other things, “a history of unpaid debts” against Mr. Wilson. The Article
states that the Wilsons are alleged to have borrowed “roughly $1.9 million”
from Mr. and Mrs. Lougheed, much of which purportedly remained unpaid at the
time of publication. The subject loans at issue were alleged to have been made
at various times between 1989 and 2006 to assist the Wilsons in purchasing the
six properties.

[
27
]

Although the allegedly defamatory content in the
Article goes well beyond the allegations of the Wilsons’ indebtedness to the
Lougheeds, the scope of this application is limited to those particular
matters.

Reasons for Judgment in the
WVA
Action

[
28
]

In the Reasons, Ballance J. thoroughly reviewed
the evidence regarding the acquisition of the six properties and the Property
Advances. Her findings may be summarized as follows:

The Jefferson Avenue property

[
29
]

The Wilsons purchased the Jefferson Avenue property
in November of 1989. The purchase price of $295,000 was financed entirely
by Mrs. Lougheed and both Mr. and Ms. Wilson’s names were registered on title. The
Wilsons granted Mrs. Lougheed a registered mortgage in the amount of $168,000. The
following spring, Mrs. Lougheed loaned the Wilsons another $30,000 so that they
could add a basement suite to the property.

[
30
]

According to the mortgage document, the Wilsons
were to make monthly payments in the amount of $1,502.74. However, Ballance J.
found that Mrs. Lougheed did not actually expect the Wilsons to adhere to this
payment scheme, given their financial situation at the time. Instead, she and Mr.
Wilson worked out a more affordable payment in the range of $550 to $600 per
month. Madam Justice Ballance concluded that Mrs. Lougheed was perfectly
content with their payment record and with the financial arrangement overall.

[
31
]

A few months after the purchase of the Gordon
Avenue property, the Wilsons sold the Jefferson Avenue property for $300,000. From
the sale proceeds, the sum of $193,539.55 was paid to Mrs. Lougheed. According
to Mrs. Lougheed’s records, the amount owing to her was closer to $207,000. However,
the preponderance of the evidence indicated that Mrs. Lougheed did not consider
the alleged deficiency to be an account receivable or an indebtedness that she
planned to collect.

The Gordon Avenue property

[
32
]

In the spring of 1991, Mrs. Lougheed, who was
assisting the Wilsons in their house-hunting efforts, located the Gordon Avenue
property and facilitated its acquisition by paying the purchase price of
$560,000 on Ms. Wilson’s behalf. Title was registered in Ms. Wilson’s name
alone and on that basis Mrs. Lougheed did not require the Wilsons to sign a
mortgage or provide any other form of security. Moreover Mrs. Lougheed did not
require the Wilsons to make monthly payments toward the purchase price. The
terms of any repayment were left vague and undefined. As of 2001, there was no
account receivable recorded in Mrs. Lougheed’s records with respect to the Gordon
Avenue property.

[
33
]

Madam Justice Ballance ultimately concluded that
Mrs. Lougheed had gifted the Gordon Avenue property to Ms. Wilson and that

Mr.
Lougheed was aware of the gift.

The Lawson Avenue property

[
34
]

Mrs. Lougheed purchased the Lawson Avenue property
in 1986 for the price of $171,000. For many years, she rented it at a
discounted rate to various relatives and family friends.

[
35
]

On October 1, 2001, Mrs. Lougheed transferred
the Lawson Avenue property to Ms. Wilson.

[
36
]

Mrs. Lougheed and Mr. Wilson discussed how the
title would be held. They agreed that Ms. Wilson would be the sole owner of the
Lawson Avenue property and that Mrs. Lougheed would not require a formal
mortgage or other form of security if title was registered in Ms. Wilson’s name
alone.

[
37
]

The price of $171,000 was to be paid in full
within one year. Madam Justice Ballance found that the parties did not make any
firm financial arrangements beyond a general understanding that Ms. Wilson
would acquire title to the property for the sum that Mrs. Lougheed had
originally paid for it, even though its value at the time was estimated to have
appreciated significantly. The purchase price was to be paid out of the
proceeds of the Gordon Avenue property, which was expected to be sold within
the year.

[
38
]

In June 2002, the Gordon Avenue property was
sold for $795,000. The Court found, at para. 123, that: “As had been agreed,
[Ms. Wilson] eventually paid her mother the sum of $171,000, or thereabouts,
for Lawson Avenue out of the proceeds of sale she received from Gordon Avenue.”

[
39
]

On the evidence, Ballance J. concluded that Mrs.
Lougheed was perfectly content with this arrangement and that as far as she was
concerned Ms. Wilson owed nothing further with respect to it.

The Pemberton Valley property

[
40
]

In November 2002, Ms. Wilson, with a view
to one day building an equestrian centre and possibly a residence, acquired a
16-acre property in the Pemberton Valley. She applied $380,000 of the sale
proceeds from the Gordon Avenue property to purchase this property. Title was
registered in Ms. Wilson’s name alone.

The Whistler property

[
41
]

In December 1990, the Lougheeds jointly
purchased a condominium in Whistler (the “Whistler property”) for the sum of
$202,200.

[
42
]

On February 4, 2003, the Lougheeds executed a
transfer document conveying title to the Whistler property to Ms. Wilson alone.

[
43
]

Madam Justice Ballance found that Mr. Wilson and
Mr. Lougheed agreed on the purchase price of $450,000, and that the details of
the payment schedule were left to be determined between Mr. Wilson and Mrs. Lougheed.

[
44
]

Although the “Whistler Payment Schedule” set the
monthly payments at $2,899.36 and incorporated an interest component in the
calculation of the monthly amount, Mr. Wilson and Mrs. Lougheed agreed that the
Wilsons’ monthly payments were to be applied in their entirety against the
principal amount of the loan. Interest would not be payable.

[
45
]

Mrs. Lougheed prepared a separate document
recording the Wilsons’ payments for the Whistler property which payments were
not made every month. The Court found there was no agreement that the Whistler
Property Loan would be repaid by a certain date.

[
46
]

With respect to the terms of repayment, Ballance
J. found as follows, at para. 151:

[151]    This
was not an arm’s length commercial transaction. It was a sweetheart family
arrangement between wealthy parents and their daughter and son-in-law. I
conclude that much like all of Norma’s financial dealings with the Wilsons,
other than ensuring the purchase price was acceptable to William and reaching
an agreement on the monthly amount payable, there was a lack of formality
surrounding the repayment of the loan. Blair and Norma left the terms of
repayment loosely defined along the lines that the Wilsons would do their best
to pay the agreed monthly amount.

[
47
]

With respect to the payments made by the Wilsons
on the Whistler Property the Court found at paras. 143-144 and 309-310:

[143]    Norma’s Whistler Accounting shows
that although the Whistler Property was transferred into Kelly’s name the first
week of February 2003, the Wilsons’ payments did not begin until May 2003. Two
cheques were evidently returned for non-sufficient funds in 2003. There was no
evidence that Norma or William sought to recoup those missed payments.

[144]    The
Wilsons typically paid by supplying Norma with several post-dated cheques and
rounded up many of their monthly payments to $2,900 or $3,000. They made twelve
monthly payments in 2004, ten payments in 2005 and seven payments in 2006.
Payments up to an including July 2006 were reflected in Norma’s Whistler
Accounting, although four more payments were made after that time.

...

[309]    On
December 6, 2006 - after the October conversation - Norma deposited a cheque
for $3000 received from the Wilsons relative to the Whistler property loan. I
conclude that the cheque deposited by Norma in December was one of the many
post-dated cheques from the Wilsons and had likely been in Norma’s possession
for several months. I accept further that Norma deposited that cheque
inadvertently along with a batch of other post-dated cheques.

[310]    A few
days later, the Wilsons’ December cheque was returned by the bank NSF. There is
no evidence that Norma ever raised the matter of the NSF cheque with Kelly or
Blair, or thereafter discussed with them the status of future payments against
the Whistler Property loan or sought further payments in the form of additional
post-dated cheques...

[
48
]

The Court concluded that Mrs. Lougheed did not
forgive the Whistler Property loan. The balance owing on the loan as of the
date of Mrs. Lougheed’s death was determined to be $350,703.84. Accordingly, Ms.
Wilson was ordered to repay that sum, together with pre-judgment interest, in
equal proportions to the Estate and to Mr. Lougheed personally.

The Roberts Creek property

[
49
]

Ms. Wilson listed the Pemberton Valley property
for sale in late 2005. The listing price was $599,000.

[
50
]

Mr. Wilson was elected to Parliament on January 23,
2006. In the summer of 2006, Ms. Wilson and Mrs. Lougheed began looking for a
new acreage within Mr. Wilson’s political riding on the Sunshine Coast, which
would in effect replace the Pemberton Valley property. Mrs. Lougheed discovered
a suitable 10-acre lot of bare land in the Roberts Creek area, which had not
been advertised in the usual multiple listing publications. The asking price
was $428,000.

[
51
]

In discussions between Ms. Wilson and Mrs. Lougheed,
it was agreed that the Lougheeds would advance Ms. Wilson the purchase price,
which she would repay from the sale proceeds of the Pemberton Valley property. The
proposed arrangement for bridge financing was subject to Mr. Lougheed’s
approval.

[
52
]

With respect to the terms of the parties’ financing
arrangement for the acquisition of the Roberts Creek property the Court found
that the payment of the purchase price was structured as follows: Mrs. Lougheed
provided a personal cheque in the amount of $16,000 for the deposit and issued
a cheque from a Norbill Investments account in the amount of $445,710.29 for
the balance of the purchase price and closing costs. On the same day, title was
registered in Ms. Wilson’s name alone. On the totality of the evidence, the Court
concluded that the parties had agreed that the Roberts Creek loan would not
become due until after the Pemberton Valley property was sold.

[
53
]

The court found that as of trial the total amount
owing in respect of the loan was $461,719.29. The court concluded that $16,000 was
due to the Estate and the balance of the loan was owed to Norbill Investments. The
loan, which bears no interest, is payable on the sale of the Pemberton Valley
property, which as of the date of trial had not yet sold.

[
54
]

In discussing the purchase of the Roberts Creek property
with her parents, Ms. Wilson did not disclose that she had granted a number of
collateral mortgages against the Pemberton Valley property, the Lawson Avenue
property, and the Whistler property in favour of various financial institutions
(the “Collateral Mortgages”). The Court found that Ms. Wilson’s handling of
these transactions was attributable to her naiveté and inexperience with
financial matters. The Court concluded that Ms. Wilson did not intentionally
misrepresent the timing of the sale of the Pemberton Valley property to her
parents in order to secure bridge financing for the acquisition of the Roberts
Creek property.

Collateral Mortgages

[
55
]

While initially on this application there was
some controversy as to whether the findings on the particulars of the
Collateral Mortgages were the subject of this application, the applicant’s
counsel confirmed in his oral submissions that he was not seeking any orders
relating to this matter. I therefore have not considered the matter in these
reasons.

The Correction

[
56
]

On January 23, 2011, approximately three weeks
after the
WVA
Action was decided,
The Province
printed the
Correction, which states as follows:

Update to a
Province

article on Blair Wilson on Oct. 28, 2007: In a Dec. 31, 2010, judgment of
the B.C. Supreme Court regarding the estate of Blair Wilson’s mother-in-law,
Norma Lougheed, it was held that all money advanced by the Lougheeds to
purchase properties was repaid to a degree acceptable to Norma Lougheed or
eventually gifted to Blair Wilson’s wife, Kelly, except the Whistler and
Roberts Creek properties, on which a total of approximately $812,000 remains
owing by Kelly Wilson. As noted in the original article, all current properties
are in Kelly Wilson’s name. The Pemberton Valley property was not purchased
with money advanced by the Lougheeds, but with the sale proceeds of the Gordon
Avenue home, which had been paid for by the Lougheeds. The $22,480 transaction
in April of 2007 was not a loan from Norma Lougheed to Blair Wilson, but a
repayment to Blair Wilson of money he had loaned his election campaign fund. Norma
Lougheed had also loaned the campaign approximately $16,000 in preceding
months, which was repaid by Blair Wilson out of the $22,480. The online version
of this article has been updated and corrected.

Analysis

[
57
]

There is no dispute as to the legal principles
which govern the disposition of this application.

Rule 9-5: Striking Pleadings

[
58
]

It is common ground that the onus on an
application to strike pleadings under the current R. 9-5(1) is the same as
under the former R. 19(24): it must be “plain and obvious” that the pleadings should
be struck. With respect to R. 9-5(1)(d) specifically, the Court of Appeal in
World
Wide Treasure Adventures Inc. v. Trivia Games Inc. et. al.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1428 (BC CA)
, 68
B.C.A.C. 241 (B.C.C.A.) at para.
37
, affirmed that on an application to
strike pleadings based on the applicability of
res judicata,
the
applicant must establish that it is “plain and obvious” that the doctrine of
res
judicata
applies to the impugned pleading.

[
59
]

The threshold for striking pleadings is high and
the test articulated in the authorities is to be applied stringently:
Ontario
(Pension Board) v. Ball
,
2010 BCSC 1267
at para.
21
.

[
60
]

The test for an application to strike under R.
9-5(1)(c) is the same as it is under R. 9-5(1)(a),(b) or (d) - it must be plain
and obvious that the pleadings at issue may prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial of the proceeding:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
) 266 (B.C.S.C.)
at para.
47
.

Res Judicata

[
61
]

Res judicata
is a
core doctrine of our Canadian justice system. The policy objectives underlying
res
judicata
are well established and can be distilled as follows - there is an
interest in putting an end to litigation and no person should be twice vexed by
the same cause of action:
Foreman v. Niven,
2009 BCSC 1476

at para.

9
;
Giles v. Westminster Savings Credit Union,
2006 BCSC 1600
at para.
26

(the relevant portions of which were ultimately affirmed on appeal:
2010 BCCA
282
). Notwithstanding the importance of these objectives, they must be balanced
with the competing principle that litigants should not be deprived of their
right to have their cases decided on the merits:
Cliffs Over Maple Bay
Investments (Re),

2011 BCCA 180
at para.
26
.

[
62
]

The Court in
Tylon Steepe Homes Ltd. v. Pont
,

2011 BCSC 385
, appeals quashed on other grounds,
2011 BCCA 162
, provides the
following formulation of the doctrine of
res judicata
at para. 52:

... Where a
cause or a fundamental issue has been decided, it is said to be
res judicata

and, absent special circumstances, is precluded from being adjudged a second
time. When
res judicata
applies, a litigant is estopped by the prior
suit from proceeding in the subsequent action. The maxim has traditionally been
regarded as an exclusionary rule of evidence. The paramount policy considerations
include the avoidance of duplicative litigation, potential inconsistent results
and inconclusive proceedings. Finality to litigation is the prime objective.
(Internal citations omitted.)

[
63
]

The doctrine of
res judicata
has two
branches: issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. Relitigation

may
be precluded in relation to an entire cause of action or with respect to a
discrete issue. The essential principles of
res judicata
apply, albeit
with modifications, to defences previously litigated as well:
Tylon Steepe,

at para. 53.

[
64
]

In this case

the applicant grounds his
submissions in the principles of issue estoppel.

[
65
]

There are three criteria which must be satisfied
in order to successfully invoke issue estoppel:

(a)    that the same question has been decided and was fundamental,
as opposed to collateral or incidental, to the decision;

(b)    that the decision in the first proceeding said to create the
estoppel was final; and

(c)     the parties to both proceedings must be the same or their
privies.

(See
Angle v. Minister of National
Revenue
,
1974 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248;
Grdic v. The Queen
,
1985 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R.
810;
Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc.
,
2001 SCC 44
)

[
66
]

I turn to address the requirement that the
parties invoking issue estoppel must establish that the parties to the current
and prior proceeding are the same or their privies.

[
67
]

Who constitutes a privy at law? The concept of “privity”
is somewhat elastic and the degree of interest which will give rise to privity
cannot be stated categorically:
Danyluk
at para.
60
.

[
68
]

In
Giles,
Sigurdson J. cited the
definition of privity provided by Donald J. Lange,
The Doctrine of Res
Judicata in Canada
, Third Edition (Markham, ON: LexisNexis Canada Inc.,
2010) at 83-84:

A privy of a
party has been variously defined in issue estoppel cases. Privity can be one of
blood, title, or interest. Before a person can be a privy of a party, there
must be community or privity of interest between them, or a unity of interest
between them. They cannot be different in substance. A person who is privy in
interest to a party in an action and has notice of that action is equally bound
by the findings in that action. The privy must have notice of the previous
proceeding to be bound by it. A privy is a person who has a right to
participate with a party in the proceeding or who has a participatory interest
in its outcome. A person who has no right to participate as a party in a
proceeding lacks a due process requirement to make a finding of privity of
interest. To determine whether a person has a participatory interest in the
outcome of the proceeding is to determine whether the outcome could affect the
liability of that person. Privity requires parallel interest in the merits of
the proceeding, not simply a financial interest in the result.

[
69
]

I turn to consider the applicability of issue
estoppel, and in particular the requirement for mutuality, to the circumstances
of this case.

[
70
]

The first question is essentially this: were the
Canwest Defendants, who are named parties in the Defamation Action, either
parties or privies of Mr. Lougheed in the
WVA
Action?

[
71
]

The Canwest Defendants assert that they did not
attend the trial of the
WVA
Action and maintain that they are not
properly characterized as parties to that action.

[
72
]

As mentioned earlier, the Canwest Defendants
were named as defendants in the defamation counterclaim in the Debt Action
which was set for trial at the same time as the
WVA
Action. However, it
was an express term of the Consent Order that Mr. Wilson’s defamation
counterclaim and the debt claims of Mr. Lougheed against Mr. Wilson be severed
and tried separately from the proceedings before Ballance J. The effect of the
Consent Order was to sever the entirety of the Defamation Action and the claims
in the Debt Action that relate to Mr. Wilson in order that these claims could
be tried separately from the
WVA
claim and the debt claim against Ms.
Wilson. The clear objective of that order was efficiency and to limit the
issues and the parties in the proceedings before Ballance J.

[
73
]

Any obligation the Canwest Defendants may have
had to participate in the
WVA
Action was terminated by the Consent
Order. Nonetheless, the applicant asserts that because the Canwest Defendants
chose not to participate in the
WVA
Action, they are now estopped by
res
judicata
from making a full defence in the current proceeding. To argue as the
applicant does, that the Canwest Defendants were initially parties to the
underlying litigation and, as such, had the opportunity to attend those
proceedings, and to examine witnesses on matters relevant to their defamation
defences, but chose not to, violates the clear objective of the Consent Order.

[
74
]

In the result, I conclude that for the purposes
of the application of issue estoppel, the Canwest Defendants were not parties
to the
WVA
Action.

[
75
]

Having concluded that the Canwest Defendants
were not parties, the matter turns on whether the Canwest Defendants, who are
named as co-defendants by counterclaim in the Defamation Action, shared a
privity of interests with Mr. Lougheed in the
WVA
Action. For the
reasons that follow, I am not persuaded that they did.

[
76
]

Firstly, I note that although there was some
controversy at the hearing on the point, the record does not show that the
Canwest Defendants were served with the Notice of Trial for the
WVA

Action. The authorities mandate that the Canwest Defendants must have had
notice of the trial in the
WVA
Action in order to be bound as privies by
the judgment in that proceeding:
West Moberly First Nations v. British
Columbia,
2007 BCSC 1324
at paras.
23-24
.

[
77
]

Moreover, I accept the Canwest Defendants’
assertion that with respect to the issues adjudicated upon by the Court in the
WVA

Action, they did not share a community of interest with Mr. Lougheed, the
Estate, or Norbill Investments. They had no stake whatsoever in the outcome of
Ms. Wilson’s action under the
WVA
or in Mr. Lougheed’s claims in debt
against Ms. Wilson. A successful result for Mr. Lougheed conferred no direct
benefit to them.

[
78
]

In the end, I find that there is not a
sufficient degree of identification between the Canwest Defendants and Mr. Lougheed
such that it would be just to hold that the Canwest Defendants are privies of Mr.
Lougheed.

[
79
]

In the result, I conclude that the doctrine of issue
estoppel is not applicable in this case. In view of my findings on this point
it is not necessary to consider whether the other constituent elements of issue
estoppel have been established.

Collateral Attack

[
80
]

Contrary to the applicant’s submissions, the
circumstances of this case do not engage the rule against collateral attack.

[
81
]

On the authorities it is clear that the focus of
the rule is on precluding attempts to indirectly reverse, vary, or nullify a
court order. The rule is anchored in the principle articulated by
Binnie J. at para. 20 in
Danyluk
,
“that a judicial order pronounced
by a court of competent jurisdiction should not be brought into question in
subsequent proceedings except those provided by law for the express purpose of
attacking it”.

[
82
]

There is no suggestion whatsoever that in the
Defamation Action the respondents seek to attack the legal force of the order
made in the
WVA
Action. In the circumstances of this case the more
appropriate approach is to consider the applicability of the doctrine of abuse
of process.

Abuse of Process

[
83
]

Modern Canadian courts have developed the
evolving and flexible doctrine of abuse of process to preclude relitigation in
circumstances where the strict requirements of
res judicata
are not met
- typically the requirement of mutuality - but where permitting the litigation
to proceed would nonetheless violate the integrity of the adjudicative process.
As observed by the trial judge in
Tylon Steepe,
at para. 79
,

abuse of process “finds it roots in the court’s residual discretion to prevent
an abuse of process”. The Supreme Court of Canada in
Toronto (City) v.
C.U.P.E. Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at para.
37
, summarized the fundamental
underpinnings of the doctrine as encompassing the vital principles of judicial
economy, consistency of results, finality to litigation and the integrity of
the administration of justice.

[
84
]

In
C.U.P.E.,
the Court held that an
employee who had been criminally convicted of sexual assault was barred from
contending in a subsequent labour arbitration that the assault did not occur.
The Court affirmed that the primary focus of the doctrine of abuse of process
is on the integrity of the adjudicative process and not on the motives of the
parties. Madam Justice Arbour, writing for the majority, set out the following
helpful formulation at para. 51:

51        Rather
than focus on the motive or status of the parties, the doctrine of abuse of
process concentrates on the integrity of the adjudicative process. Three
preliminary observations are useful in that respect. First, there can be no
assumption that relitigation will yield a more accurate result than the
original proceeding. Second, if the same result is reached in the subsequent
proceeding, the relitigation will prove to have been a waste of judicial
resources as well as an unnecessary expense for the parties and possibly an
additional hardship for some witnesses. Finally,
if the result in the
subsequent proceeding is different from the conclusion reached in the first on
the very same issue, the inconsistency, in and of itself, will undermine the
credibility of the entire judicial process, thereby diminishing its authority,
its credibility and its aim of finality.
[Emphasis added.]

[
85
]

Recently, in
Petrelli v. Lindell Beach
Holiday Resort Ltd.,
2011 BCCA 367
at para.
71
, the Court of Appeal affirmed
that relitigation of an issue that has been finally determined in a previous
proceeding challenges the integrity of the adjudicative function of the courts
in the following two respects:

... First, the
duplication of efforts results in inefficient use of judicial resources. This
inefficiency directly impacts the ability of the courts to function. It also
tends to diminish public respect for the judicial process. Second, in opening
up the possibility of inconsistent findings of fact, relitigation of an issue
diminishes the credibility authority of judgments.

[
86
]

As with issue estoppel, the requirement of
finality is a constituent element of the doctrine of abuse of process as it
pertains to relitigation. In discussing this requirement, Roscoe J.A. in
Lienaux
v. 2301072 Nova Scotia Ltd.,
2005 NSCA 97
at para.
32
, leave to appeal to
SCC refused, [2006] 1 S.C.R. xi,

cited the following excerpts from

Donald
J. Lange,
The Doctrine of Res Judicata in Canada
(Markham, ON:
Butterworths Canada Ltd., 2000), at 77:

The decision must be a final decision. A
final decision for the purposes of issue estoppel is a decision which
conclusively determines the questions between the parties...

The test for
finality for issue estoppel, therefore, is that a decision is final when the
decision-making forum pronouncing it has no further jurisdiction to rehear the
question or to vary or rescind the finding.

The “Same Question” Test

[
87
]

It is essential to the analysis to appreciate
that in addition to the finality requirement, the “same question” test must
also be satisfied in order to invoke the doctrine of abuse of process regarding
relitigation. The Court in
Petrelli
, at para.
72
, stated that the
integrity of the adjudicative process is challenged when a court is invited to
come to a “different finding of fact on an issue than was reached in previous
litigation”.

[
88
]

Mr. Justice Binnie’s formulation in
Danyluk

of the matters to which estoppel applies in the context of an issue estoppel
case informs the analysis of the “same question” test in the case of abuse of
process by relitigation (at para. 24):

This
description of the issues subject to estoppel (“
[a]ny right, question or
fact distinctly put in issue and directly determined”)
is more stringent
than the formulation in some of the older cases for cause of action estoppel
(e.g., “all matters which were, or might properly have been, brought into
litigation”,
Farwell, supra
, at p. 558). Dickson J. (later
C.J.), speaking for the majority in
Angle
, supra
, at p. 255,
subscribed to the more stringent definition for the purpose of issue estoppel.
“It will not suffice” he said, “if the question arose collaterally or incidentally
in the earlier proceedings or is one which must be inferred by argument from
the judgment.”  The question out of which the estoppel is said to arise must
have been “fundamental to the decision arrived at” in the earlier proceeding.
In other words, as discussed below,
the estoppel extends to the material
facts and the conclusions of law or of mixed fact and law (“the questions”)
that were necessarily (even if not explicitly) determined in the earlier
proceedings.
[Emphasis added, internal citations omitted.]

[
89
]

I turn to address the application of these
principles to the circumstances of this case. The Applicant asserts that the
doctrine of issue estoppel is applicable because the common issue to both
proceedings, and which he says was determined in the
WVA
Action, “is the
indebtedness of either Kelly or Blair Wilson in relation to the six properties
to either William or the Estate of the late Norma Lougheed”. In my view the
applicant’s postulation

misconceives the test for striking the defences
in this case. Rather the disposition of this matter turns on whether the
impugned defences in the Defamation Action raise triable issues which fall
outside the ambit of the judgment of Ballance J. in the
WVA
Action.

[
90
]

Before turning to the analysis it is necessary to
identify the constituent elements of each of the impugned defences. It is
common ground that each of these defences depends, in varying degrees, upon
establishing the truth of the underlying assertions.

Justification

[
91
]

The test for justification in respect of the
publication of an allegedly defamatory statement is whether the statement was “substantially
true” or “true in substance”. However it is key to observe that the defence of
justification turns on the overall “sting” of the defamation, not whether the
published words were true in every respect:
Jay v. Hollinger Canadian
Newspapers, Limited Partnership,
2002 BCSC 1655
;
Miller v. Canadian
Broadcasting Corp.,
2003 BCSC 258
,
P.G. Restaurant Ltd. v. Cariboo Press
(1969) Ltd.,

2005 BCCA 210
at para
33
, application for re-hearing
dismissed,
2005 BCCA 288
, leave to appeal to SCC refused, [2005] 3 S.C.R. vii. Minor
inaccuracies which do not affect the substantial truth of the statement or add
materially to its defamatory quality may be overlooked: Raymond E. Brown,
The
Law of Defamation in Canada,
2
nd
Edition, Vol. 3, loose-leaf
(Toronto: Carswell, 2009) at 10-40 to 10-45 [Brown on Defamation].

[
92
]

The applicant’s primary contention is that the
pleas of justification should be struck in their entirety from the respondents’
Statements of Defences.

[
93
]

The respondents forcefully assert that the issue
in the Defamation Action is not whether Mr. Wilson was in fact indebted to Mr. Lougheed
or the Estate when the allegedly defamatory statements were published; it is
whether the overall defamatory “sting” of the Article, which dealt with Mr.
Wilson’s debts - including to other unrelated parties - was true in substance.

[
94
]

In my view the defence of justification raises
issues which were not determined in the
WVA
Action. While significant
elements of the Article relate to the allegations of indebtedness by the
Wilsons to the Lougheeds, the substance of the Article patently goes beyond
matters that were before the Court in the
WVA
Action. The Article also
includes references to Mr. Wilson’s business ventures, business debts, and
alleged breaches of the
Canada Elections Act,
S.C. 2000, c. 9. It
follows that the issue of whether the statements in the Article were “justified”
cannot be reduced to a question of assessing the accuracy of the allegations of
indebtedness to the Lougheeds described therein in light of the findings in the

WVA
Action.

[
95
]

Moreover I am satisfied that in order to
determine the overall sting of the alleged defamation, the Court at trial will
be required to assess the Article in its entirety. I agree with the Canwest
Defendants that the determination of the overall sting of the Article and the
determination of whether it is substantially true are not suitable for
disposition on a pleadings motion. These determinations, which lie at the heart
of the Defamation Action, raise triable issues.

[
96
]

In the result, I conclude that it would be
inappropriate at this stage to strike the pleas of justification.

Fair Comment

[
97
]

In contrast to justification, which pertains to statements
of fact, the defence of fair comment protects statements of opinion, which
includes any “deduction, inference, conclusion, criticism, judgment, remark or
observation which is generally incapable of proof”:
Ross v. New Brunswick
Teachers’ Assn.,
2001 NBCA 62
at para.
56
, cited in
Grant v.
Torstar Corp.,
2009 SCC 61
at para.
31
.

[
98
]

The test for fair comment was reformulated by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson,
2008 SCC 40
,
and summarized by McLachlin C.J.C. in
Grant v. Torstar Corp.

2009 SCC 61

at para.
31
. Under the current framework, a defendant claiming fair
comment must establish the following:

(a)    the comment was on a matter of public interest;

(b)    the comment was based on fact;

(c)     the comment, though it can include inferences of fact, must
be recognizable as comment;

(d)    the comment satisfies the following objective test: could any
person honestly express that opinion on the proved facts? and

(e)    the defendant in making the comment was not actuated by
express malice.

[
99
]

The requirement that the comment be based on
fact does not mean that the fair comment defence is bound to fail if any aspect
of the factual basis is untrue. A plea of fair comment will succeed if the
facts which are shown to be true are sufficient to support the comment:
Kemsley
v. Foot and
others
[1952] 1 All E.R. 501 (H.L.)
. Lord Denning observed in
London
Artists Ltd. v. Littler
,
[1969] 2 All E.R. 193 (C.A.) at 198,
that “the
commentator must get [the] basic facts right. The basic facts are those which
go to the pith and substance of the matter”.

[
100
]

The applicant seeks to strike the pleas of fair comment in their
entirety, except paragraph 11 (which references Mr. Wilson’s businesses and
finances) and subparagraph 13(a) (which references Mr. Wilson’s involvement in
the Pan Smak pizza business) of the Canwest Defendants’ Statement of Defence.
The respondents contend that the comments in the Article - for example, Mr.
Lougheed’s expressed opinion that Mr. Wilson was “not fit for public office” -
are protected by the defence of fair comment. They argue firstly that this
defence does not necessarily fail if aspects of the factual foundation for the
comment are not true. Secondly, they emphasize that the factual foundation
supporting the comment in the Article is not restricted to the factual matrix
of the Property Advances. Rather, they contend that the “comments” in the
Article are anchored in a broader framework of factual underpinnings.

[
101
]

I agree that the court in the
WVA
Action found some but not
all of the facts pertaining to the factual substrata for the comment. In
determining the applicability of the defence of fair comment it is clear the
court will be required to decide questions which were not decided in the
WVA

Action.  In the result, I cannot conclude that the defence of fair comment is
bound to fail based on the doctrine of abuse of process.

Fair Reporting

[
102
]

The common law has long recognized a defence of fair and accurate
reporting in respect of judicial proceedings. The analysis of this defence does
not mandate an examination of the truth

of the charges made during the
proceedings but rather the accuracy of the reporting of proceedings. The
rationale for the defence is rooted in the right of public to be informed of
all aspects of proceedings to which it has the right of access:
Hill v. Church
of Scientology of Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130 at para.
151
.

[
103
]

Brown on Defamation sets out the following
articulation of the test for fair reporting at 14-2 and 14-27 to 14-28:

Fairness does not require that the report be
literally true so long as it is substantially correct...The report must be
confined to proceedings that took place in open court, and extends to papers
and documents filed with, and the comments of all those properly involved in,
judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings at every level of jurisdiction. (14-2)

The “report
need be neither exhaustive and detailed nor perfectly precise in language”. It
is sufficient if the report is true in substance. (14-27 to 14-28)

[
104
]

The right to report on court proceedings extends to pleadings and
court documents filed before trial. Where the filing of court documents occurs
after the litigant or lawyer describes their intention to file those court
documents, fair reporting privilege can apply:
Hill
at para.152.

The
courts have cautioned that considerable care must be taken in reporting on such
documents to minimize the risk of harm to innocent persons who may have no
opportunity to reply to potentially defamatory statements:
Taylor-Wright v.
CHBC-TV,
2000 BCCA 629
, var’d on other grounds
2001 BCCA 298
;
M.D.
Mineralsearch Inc. v. East Kootenay Newspapers Ltd.,
2002 BCCA 42
.

[
105
]

The authorities do not require that the entire proceeding be
reported at one time “so long as a substantially fair report is eventually made
”:

Brown on Defamation

at

14-43
.

[
106
]

The Canwest Defendants argue that insofar as the Article describes
allegations of the Wilsons’ indebtedness to the Lougheeds, it refers to Mr.
Lougheed’s statement that he and his late wife were owed in the range of $1.9
million by the Wilsons. They point out that Mr. Lougheed commenced an action
seeking recovery of those monies within a few months of the Article’s
publication. The Canwest Defendants maintain that the discontinuance of some of
those claims in the Debt Action does not alter the essential fact that at the
material time debts were alleged in respect of all of the various property
loans referred to in the Article. Finally, they emphasize that shortly after
the judgment was rendered,
The Province
accurately reported the judicial
conclusions on these matters in the Correction.

[
107
]

In light of the governing legal principles, the defence of fair
reporting clearly raises triable issues which were not determined in the
WVA

Action. It is not plain and obvious on this pleadings motion that the defence
of fair reporting should be struck based on the doctrine of abuse of process.

Summary

[
108
]

In summary on this issue I conclude that the defences of
justification, fair comment, and fair reporting raise triable issues which fall
outside the ambit of the judgment of Ballance J. It is not plain and obvious
that the doctrine of issue estoppel or abuse of process can be invoked to preclude
the respondents from relying on these defences in the Defamation Action. The
applicant has failed to establish that the defences should be struck pursuant
to Rule 9-5 (1)(d).

[
109
]

Further, the applicant has failed to establish that the impugned
defences may otherwise prejudice, embarrass, or delay the applicant’s
opportunity for a fair trial such that they ought to be struck under R.
9-5(1)(c).

[
110
]

The applicant’s submissions address the merits of the respondents’
defences. Having concluded that the defences should not be struck, it is not
for this Court on this application to consider the merits of the defences.

[
111
]

In the result, the application to strike the defences of
justification, fair comment, and fair reporting in whole or in part is
dismissed.

THE ALTERNATIVE RELIEF SOUGHT

[
112
]

In the alternative, the applicant - who participated in the
WVA

Action, albeit not as a named party - seeks an order that the parties are bound
by Ballance J.’s findings.

[
113
]

To put the issue properly in context, I turn to address the principles
which inform the analysis of a claim brought pursuant to the
WVA
.

[
114
]

The key provision of the
WVA
is s. 2. That section provides
that if, in the court’s opinion, a will fails to make adequate provision for
the proper maintenance and support of the testator’s spouse or children, the
court is empowered, in its discretion, to vary the will to make provision that
it considers adequate, just and equitable in the circumstances.

[
115
]

Tataryn v. Tataryn Estate
,
1994 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, [1994] 2
S.C.R. 807, is the governing authority in British Columbia on the
WVA
.
Madam Justice McLachlin (as she then was), writing for the Court, articulated
the relevant considerations and principles that animate the application of the
WVA
:

Brown v. Ferguson,

2010 BCSC 1890
.

[
116
]

Madam Justice McLachlin clarified that the adequacy of the
testamentary provision in a will is measured on an objective standard, assessed
in light of current societal legal and moral norms. Pursuant to the principles
articulated in
Tataryn
, legal norms are the obligations that would be imposed
upon the testator during his or her life if the question of provision for a
claimant’s spouse or child were to arise. A testator’s moral duties are to be
grounded in “society’s reasonable expectations of what a judicious person would
do in the circumstances, by reference to contemporary community standards”:
Tataryn

at 820-821, cited in
Brown
at para.
96
.

[
117
]

The findings in the
WVA
Action regarding the Property
Advances were material facts for the purpose of assessing Ms. Wilson’s claim
under the
WVA
. Madam Justice Ballance held that Ms. Wilson’s claim under
the
WVA
turned on “the determination of the nature and event of the
moral obligation Norma may have owed Kelly,” and whether that moral duty had
been negated. As referred to in paragraph 385 of the Reasons, it is well
settled on the authorities that where a testatrix has made
inter vivos

gifts or conferred
inter vivos
benefits on a claimant, the moral duty of
the testatrix to that claimant may be diminished or even negated. It follows
that the Court’s findings regarding any gifts or benefits Ms. Wilson may have
received in connection with the six properties were necessary and fundamental
determinations in deciding Ms. Wilson’s claim under the
WVA
.

[
118
]

It is axiomatic that the findings with respect to the Property
Advances and the amounts owing on the Roberts Creek and Whistler properties
were fundamental to the Court’s adjudication of the debt claims against Ms.
Wilson.

[
119
]

Section 6(b) of the
WVA
empowers the court to refuse relief
to a claimant whose character or conduct disentitles that claimant to the
benefit of an order under the Act. The findings relating to Ms. Wilson’s
non-disclosure of the Collateral Mortgages to her parents were fundamental to
the Court’s consideration of section 6(b) of the
WVA
.

[
120
]

These fundamental questions which have been determined in the
WVA

Action cannot be relitigated and are binding in these proceedings.

[
121
]

Based on the principles articulated in the authorities I am
satisfied that Ballance J.’s findings on these matters were final
determinations. The Reasons and findings therein were final in that the Court
has no further jurisdiction to rehear the questions or to vary or rescind the
findings. The Reasons left nothing to be judicially determined or ascertained
thereafter. I note parenthetically that the Canwest Defendants properly
conceded this point at the hearing of the application and in their supplemental
written submissions.

[
122
]

Relitigating this matter and permitting the respondents an
opportunity to persuade a trier of fact to come to findings contrary to those
made by Ballance J. in the
WVA
Action on essential points would
constitute an abuse of the Court’s processes. It would result in an inefficient
use of judicial resources, an unnecessary expense for the parties, and in facilitating
the potential for inconsistent findings on primary facts, would undermine the
authority and finality of the previous judgment in the mind of a reasonable
observer. In my view, inconsistent findings in the subsequent action would
challenge the integrity of the adjudicative function of the courts and thereby
impugn the authority of the justice system.

[
123
]

As noted earlier, the Canwest Defendants, who
were not parties to the prior litigation, do not seek to challenge the findings
in the
WVA
Action. It would be most unjust if Mr. Lougheed, either
personally or in his representative capacity, was permitted an opportunity to
challenge the findings in the Reasons relating to the Property Advances.
Significantly, in my view, in his supplemental written submissions, which were
filed after the hearing, Mr. Lougheed formally admitted that prior to the late
Mrs. Lougheed’s death:

(i)         she forgave the loan to the Wilsons of $569,097.00 in
relation to the Gordon Avenue property;

(ii)        the loan of $171,000.00 made by the late Mrs. Lougheed
on October 2001 to enable the Wilsons to acquire the Lawson Property was repaid
by Mr. Wilson in June 2002; and

(iii)       the
Pemberton Property was paid for from the sale proceeds of the Gordon Property.

[
124
]

I am mindful of the Court’s observation in
Petrelli
,
at para.

72
,

that there are situations in which overriding concerns of fairness
to the parties require challenges to the integrity of the adjudicative function
of the courts to be tolerated. This is not one of those cases. I am not
persuaded that there are any special factors that would compel me to exercise
my discretion to refuse to apply the doctrine of abuse of process.

[
125
]

While I accept the respondents’ submissions that R. 9-5(1)(c) does
not confer jurisdiction to grant the alternative relief sought by the
applicant, I am satisfied that I have the inherent jurisdiction to make the
order.

[
126
]

In summary on this issue, this Court orders that Ballance J.’s
findings in the
WVA
Action - as they are set out earlier in these
reasons under the headings, the Jefferson Avenue property, the Gordon Avenue
property, the Lawson Avenue property, the Pemberton Valley property, the Whistler
property, and the Roberts Creek property - are binding in the Defamation
Action. The parties are barred from challenging these findings in the
Defamation Action.

[
127
]

It will remain open to the court to determine whether on these
facts, among others, the impugned defences can be sustained.

[
128
]

Given my conclusions on the applicability of the doctrine of abuse
of process, it is not necessary to address the parties’ submissions regarding
the legal significance of Mr. Lougheed, both in his personal and representative
capacities, having discontinued certain of the debt claims.

RULE 7-7(6): ORDERS ON ADMISSIONS

[
129
]

Pursuant to R. 7-7(6), which provides for orders based on
admissions, the applicant seeks an order regarding the Deathbed Loan and in
respect of Mrs. Lougheed’s Retirement Income Fund (the “RIF”).

[
130
]

An application under R. 7-7(6) can only be based on an admission
made by a party, whether by pleadings, in response to a notice to admit, or in
a statement under oath. Only a clear and deliberate concession to the opposing
party will provide a basis for an order under this Rule:
Adams v. Fairmont
Hotels & Resorts Inc.,
2008 BCCA 444
at paras.
10-11
. Although a party
who unreasonably refuses to make an admission can be penalized in costs, this
Court has no jurisdiction to compel a party to make an admission.

The Deathbed Loan

[
131
]

The applicant did not particularize with any precision what orders
he seeks regarding the Deathbed Loan; only that the Court make such an order as
“will further the objectives” of the
Rules
.

[
132
]

The relevant excerpt from the Article reads as
follows:

The final straw
for Lougheed, he says, was when Wilson asked his mother-in-law for money on her
deathbed. Lougheed has a copy of a cheque Norma wrote Blair for $22,840.82 on April
27, 2007, just a month before she died from cancer.

[
133
]

There is no mention of the Deathbed Loan in the Reasons. Given that
there has been no judicial determination on this matter, neither issue estoppel
nor abuse of process is engaged.

[
134
]

Mr. Lougheed, by way of his formal admission dated
September 28, 2011, admitted that the late Mrs. Lougheed did not write a
cheque on April 27, 2007, for $22,840.82.

[
135
]

The Canwest Defendants, while not making a formal admission under
the
Rules
, published the Correction, which states that the $22,480.82
transaction was not a loan from Mrs. Lougheed to Mr. Wilson, but a repayment to
Mr. Wilson of money he had loaned his election campaign fund.

[
136
]

I cannot conclude that the acknowledged inaccuracy regarding the
Deathbed Loan renders it plain and obvious that any of the defences of
justification, fair comment or fair reporting are bound to fail. The precise
legal effect of both the Correction and Mr. Lougheed’s formal admission on this
particular point is not properly determined on the limited evidence before the
Court on this motion. It is a triable issue.

The Retirement Income Fund

[
137
]

Prior to commencing her action under the
WVA,
Ms. Wilson
brought a summary trial application seeking payment of her mother’s RIF. On
March 20, 2009, Russell J. found that Mr. Lougheed had breached his
fiduciary duty by failing to pay Ms. Wilson, who was the designated beneficiary
of her late mother’s RIF, an amount equal to the face value of the RIF. She
granted judgment in favour of Ms. Wilson in the amount of $422,251.33 plus
interest. Upon the application of Mr. Lougheed the Court granted a partial stay
by ordering that $200,000.00 of the judgment amount be held in trust pending
the outcome of the
WVA
Action.

[
138
]

Although it was not clear at the hearing of this application
precisely what order the applicant was seeking regarding the RIF, in his
written submissions he seeks an order pursuant to R. 7-7(6) that paras. 302-305
of the Reasons - which deal generally with Ms. Wilson’s claim for payment of
the RIF -

are binding on the parties in the Defamation Action and that
“no evidence shall be called to contradict this finding of the court.”

[
139
]

In my view, it is fatal to applicant’s submissions that the RIF is
not referenced in the Notice of Application. The Notice of Application refers
exclusively to the “debt allegations” against the Wilsons. If the applicant
wishes to pursue this matter he is at liberty to file the appropriate
application materials.

140
]

]

WVA
Action which I have particularized in paragraph
